{{Short description|Measure of unpredictability of outcomes}}
The '''min-entropy''', in [[information theory]], is the smallest of the [[Rényi entropy|Rényi family]] of entropies, corresponding to the [[Rényi entropy#Min-entropy|most conservative]] way of measuring the unpredictability of a set of outcomes, as the negative logarithm of the probability of the ''most likely'' outcome.  The various Rényi entropies are all equal for a uniform distribution, but measure the unpredictability of a nonuniform distribution in different ways.  The min-entropy is never greater than the ordinary or [[Shannon entropy]] (which measures the average unpredictability of the outcomes) and that in turn is never greater than the Hartley or [[Rényi entropy#Hartley or max-entropy|max-entropy]], defined as the logarithm of the ''number'' of outcomes with nonzero probability.

As with the classical Shannon entropy and its quantum generalization, the [[von Neumann entropy]], one can define a conditional version of min-entropy.  The conditional quantum min-entropy is a one-shot, or conservative, analog of [[conditional quantum entropy]].

To interpret a conditional information measure, suppose [[Alice and Bob]] were to share a bipartite quantum state <math>\rho_{AB}</math>. Alice has access to system <math>A</math> and Bob to system <math>B</math>. The [[conditional entropy]] measures the average uncertainty Bob has about Alice's state upon sampling from his own system. The min-entropy can be interpreted as the distance of a state from a maximally entangled state.

This concept is useful in [[quantum cryptography]], in the context of [[privacy amplification]] (see for example <ref>{{cite journal | last1=Vazirani | first1=Umesh | last2=Vidick | first2=Thomas | title=Fully Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution | journal=Physical Review Letters | volume=113 | issue=14 | date=29 September 2014 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.113.140501 | article-number=140501|arxiv=1210.1810 | pmid=25325625| bibcode=2014PhRvL.113n0501V | s2cid=119299119 }}</ref>).

== Definition for classical distributions ==
If <math>P=(p_1,...,p_n)</math> is a classical finite probability distribution, its min-entropy can be defined as<ref>{{cite journal|last1=König|first1=Robert|last2=Renner|first2=Renato|author-link2=Renato Renner|last3=Schaffner|first3=Christian|year=2009|title=The Operational Meaning of Min- and Max-Entropy|journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory|publisher=Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)|volume=55|issue=9|pages=4337–4347|arxiv=0807.1338|doi=10.1109/tit.2009.2025545|issn=0018-9448|s2cid=17160454}}</ref> <math display="block">H_{\rm min}(\boldsymbol P) = \log\frac{1}{P_{\rm max}},
\qquad P_{\rm max}\equiv \max_i p_i.</math>One way to justify the name of the quantity is to compare it with the more standard definition of entropy, which reads <math>\textstyle H(\boldsymbol P)=\sum_i p_i\log(1/p_i)</math>, and can thus be written concisely as the expectation value of <math>\log (1/p_i)</math> over the distribution. If instead of taking the expectation value of this quantity we take its minimum value, we get precisely the above definition of <math>H_{\rm min}(\boldsymbol P)</math>.

From an operational perspective, the min-entropy equals the negative logarithm of the probability of successfully guessing the outcome of a random draw from <math>P</math>.
This is because it is optimal to guess the element with the largest probability and the chance of success equals the probability of that element.

== Definition for quantum states ==

A natural way to generalize "min-entropy" from classical to quantum states is to leverage the simple observation that quantum states define classical probability distributions when measured in some basis. There is however the added difficulty that a single [[quantum state]] can result in infinitely many possible probability distributions, depending on how it is measured. A natural path is then, given a quantum state <math>\rho</math>, to still define <math>H_{\rm min}(\rho)</math> as <math>\log(1/P_{\rm max}) </math>, but this time defining <math>P_{\rm max} </math> as the maximum possible probability that can be obtained measuring <math>\rho </math>, maximizing over all possible projective measurements.
Using this, one gets the operational definition that the min-entropy of <math> \rho </math> equals the negative logarithm of the probability of successfully guessing the outcome of any measurement of <math> \rho </math>.

Formally, this leads to the definition
<math display="block">H_{\rm min}(\rho) = \max_\Pi \log \frac{1}{\max_i \operatorname{tr}(\Pi_i \rho)}
= - \max_\Pi \log \max_i \operatorname{tr}(\Pi_i \rho), </math>
where we are maximizing over the set of all projective measurements <math>\Pi=(\Pi_i)_i</math>, <math>\Pi_i</math> represent the measurement outcomes in the [[POVM]] formalism, and <math>\operatorname{tr}(\Pi_i \rho)</math> is therefore the probability of observing the <math>i</math>-th outcome when the measurement is <math>\Pi</math>.

A more concise method to write the double maximization is to observe that any element of any POVM is a Hermitian operator such that <math>0\le \Pi\le I</math>, and thus we can equivalently directly maximize over these to get <math display="block">H_{\rm min}(\rho) = -
\max_{0\le \Pi\le I} \log \operatorname{tr}(\Pi \rho).</math>In fact, this maximization can be performed explicitly and the maximum is obtained when <math>\Pi</math> is the projection onto (any of) the largest eigenvalue(s) of <math>\rho</math>. We thus get yet another expression for the min-entropy as: <math display="block">H_{\rm min}(\rho) = -\log \|\rho\|_{\rm op},</math>remembering that the [[operator norm]] of a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator equals its largest eigenvalue.

== Conditional entropies ==
Let <math>\rho_{AB}</math> be a bipartite density operator on the space <math>\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B</math>. The min-entropy of <math>A</math> conditioned on <math>B</math> is defined to be
<math display="block">H_{\min}(A|B)_{\rho} \equiv -\inf_{\sigma_B}D_{\max}(\rho_{AB}\|I_A \otimes \sigma_B)</math>
where the infimum ranges over all density operators <math>\sigma_B</math> on the space <math>\mathcal{H}_B</math>. The measure <math>D_{\max}</math> is the maximum relative entropy defined as
<math display="block">D_{\max}(\rho\|\sigma) = \inf_{\lambda}\{\lambda:\rho \leq 2^{\lambda}\sigma\}</math>
The smooth min-entropy is defined in terms of the min-entropy.
<math display="block">H_{\min}^{\epsilon}(A|B)_{\rho} = \sup_{\rho'} H_{\min}(A|B)_{\rho'}</math>
where the sup and inf range over density operators <math>\rho'_{AB}</math> which are <math>\epsilon</math>-close to <math>\rho_{AB}
</math>. This measure of <math>\epsilon</math>-close is defined in terms of the purified distance
<math display="block">P(\rho,\sigma) = \sqrt{1 - F(\rho,\sigma)^2}</math>
where <math> F(\rho,\sigma)</math> is the [[fidelity of quantum states|fidelity]] measure.

These quantities can be seen as generalizations of the [[von Neumann entropy]]. Indeed, the von Neumann entropy can be expressed as
<math display="block">S(A|B)_{\rho} = \lim_{\epsilon \to 0}\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} H_{\min}^{\epsilon} (A^n|B^n)_{\rho^{\otimes n}}~.</math>
This is called the fully quantum asymptotic equipartition theorem.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Tomamichel | first1=Marco | last2=Colbeck | first2=Roger | last3=Renner | first3=Renato | title=A Fully Quantum Asymptotic Equipartition Property | journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory | publisher=Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) | volume=55 | issue=12 | year=2009 | issn=0018-9448 | doi=10.1109/tit.2009.2032797 | pages=5840–5847| arxiv=0811.1221 | s2cid=12062282 }}</ref>
The smoothed entropies share many interesting properties with the von Neumann entropy. For example, the smooth min-entropy satisfy a data-processing inequality:<ref>Renato Renner, "Security of Quantum Key Distribution", Ph.D. Thesis, Diss. ETH No. 16242 {{arxiv| quant-ph/0512258}}</ref>
<math display="block">H_{\min}^{\epsilon}(A|B)_{\rho} \geq H_{\min}^{\epsilon}(A|BC)_{\rho}~.</math>

== Operational interpretation of smoothed min-entropy ==

Henceforth, we shall drop the subscript <math>\rho</math> from the min-entropy when it is obvious from the context on what state it is evaluated.

=== Min-entropy as uncertainty about classical information ===
Suppose an agent had access to a quantum system <math>B</math> whose state <math>\rho_{B}^x</math> depends on some classical variable <math>X</math>. Furthermore, suppose that each of its elements <math>x</math> is distributed according to some distribution <math>P_X(x)</math>. This can be described by the following state over the system <math>XB</math>.
<math display="block">\rho_{XB} = \sum_x P_X (x) |x\rangle\langle x| \otimes \rho_{B}^x ,</math>
where <math>\{|x\rangle\}</math> form an orthonormal basis. We would like to know what the agent can learn about the classical variable <math>x</math>. Let <math>p_g(X|B)</math> be the probability that the agent guesses <math>X</math> when using an optimal measurement strategy
<math display="block">p_g(X|B) = \sum_x P_X(x) \operatorname{tr}(E_x \rho_B^x) ,</math>
where <math>E_x</math> is the POVM that maximizes this expression. It can be shown<ref>{{cite journal |last1=König|first1=Robert|last2=Renner|first2=Renato|author-link2=Renato Renner|last3=Schaffner|first3=Christian|year=2009|title=The Operational Meaning of Min- and Max-Entropy|journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory|publisher=Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)|volume=55|issue=9|pages=4337–4347|arxiv=0807.1338|doi=10.1109/tit.2009.2025545|issn=0018-9448|s2cid=17160454}}</ref> that this optimum can be expressed in terms of the min-entropy as
<math display="block">p_g(X|B) = 2^{-H_{\min}(X|B)}~.</math>

If the state <math>\rho_{XB}</math> is a product state i.e. <math>\rho_{XB} = \sigma_X \otimes \tau_B</math> for some density operators <math>\sigma_X</math> and <math>\tau_B</math>, then there is no correlation between the systems <math>X</math> and <math>B</math>. In this case, it turns out that <math>2^{-H_{\min}(X|B)} = \max_x P_X(x)~.</math>

Since the conditional min-entropy is always smaller than the conditional Von Neumann entropy, it follows that
<math display="block">p_g(X|B) \geq 2^{-S(A|B)_{\rho}}~.</math>

==== Min-entropy as overlap with the maximally entangled state ====

The maximally entangled state <math>|\phi^+\rangle</math> on a bipartite system <math>\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B</math> is defined as
<math display="block">|\phi^+\rangle_{AB} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} \sum_{x_A,x_B} |x_A\rangle |x_B\rangle</math>
where <math>\{|x_A\rangle\}</math> and <math>\{|x_B\rangle\}</math> form an orthonormal basis for the spaces <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> respectively.
For a bipartite quantum state <math>\rho_{AB}</math>, we define the maximum overlap with the maximally entangled state as
<math display="block">q_{c}(A|B) = d_A \max_{\mathcal{E}} F\left((I_A \otimes \mathcal{E}) \rho_{AB}, |\phi^+\rangle\langle \phi^{+}|\right)^2</math>
where the maximum is over all CPTP operations <math>\mathcal{E}</math> and <math>d_A</math> is the dimension of subsystem <math>A</math>. This is a measure of how correlated the state <math>\rho_{AB}</math> is. It can be shown that <math>q_c(A|B) = 2^{-H_{\min}(A|B)}</math>. If the information contained in <math>A</math> is classical, this reduces to the expression above for the guessing probability.

=== Proof of operational characterization of min-entropy ===

The proof is from a paper by König, Schaffner, Renner in 2008.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=König|first1=Robert|last2=Renner|first2=Renato|author-link2=Renato Renner|last3=Schaffner|first3=Christian|year=2009|title=The Operational Meaning of Min- and Max-Entropy|journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory|publisher=Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)|volume=55|issue=9|pages=4337–4347|arxiv=0807.1338|doi=10.1109/tit.2009.2025545|issn=0018-9448|s2cid=17160454}}</ref> It involves the machinery of [[semidefinite programming|semidefinite programs]].<ref>[[John Watrous (computer scientist)|John Watrous]], Theory of quantum information, Fall 2011, course notes, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~watrous/CS766/LectureNotes/07.pdf</ref> Suppose we are given some bipartite density operator <math>\rho_{AB}</math>. From the definition of the min-entropy, we have
<math display="block">H_{\min}(A|B) = - \inf_{\sigma_B} \inf_\lambda \{ \lambda | \rho_{AB} \leq 2^{\lambda}(I_A \otimes \sigma_B)\}~.</math>

This can be re-written as
<math display="block">-\log \inf_{\sigma_B} \operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_B)</math>
subject to the conditions
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\sigma_B &\geq 0, \\
I_A \otimes \sigma_B &\geq \rho_{AB}~.
\end{align}</math>

We notice that the infimum is taken over compact sets and hence can be replaced by a minimum. This can then be expressed succinctly as a semidefinite program. Consider the primal problem
<math display="block">\begin{cases}
\text{min:}\operatorname{Tr} (\sigma_B) \\
\text{subject to: } I_A \otimes \sigma_B \geq \rho_{AB} \\
\sigma_B \geq 0~.
\end{cases}</math>

This primal problem can also be fully specified by the matrices <math>(\rho_{AB},I_B,\operatorname{Tr}^*)</math> where <math>\operatorname{Tr}^*</math> is the adjoint of the partial trace over <math>A</math>. The action of <math>\operatorname{Tr}^*</math> on operators on <math>B</math> can be written as
<math display="block">\operatorname{Tr}^*(X) = I_A \otimes X~.</math>

We can express the dual problem as a maximization over operators <math>E_{AB}</math> on the space <math>AB</math> as
<math display="block">\begin{cases}
\text{max:}\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_{AB}E_{AB}) \\
\text{subject to: } \operatorname{Tr}_A(E_{AB}) = I_B \\
E_{AB} \geq 0~.
\end{cases}</math>

Using the [[Choi–Jamiołkowski isomorphism]], we can define the channel <math>\mathcal{E}</math> such that
<math display="block">d_A I_A \otimes \mathcal{E}^{\dagger}(|\phi^{+}\rangle\langle\phi^{+}|) = E_{AB}</math>
where the [[bell state]] is defined over the space <math>AA'</math>. This means that we can express the objective function of the dual problem as
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\langle \rho_{AB}, E_{AB} \rangle
&= d_A \langle \rho_{AB}, I_A \otimes \mathcal{E}^{\dagger} (|\phi^+\rangle\langle \phi^+|) \rangle \\
&= d_A \langle I_A \otimes \mathcal{E}(\rho_{AB}), |\phi^+\rangle\langle \phi^+|) \rangle
\end{align}</math>
as desired.

Notice that in the event that the system <math>A</math> is a partly classical state as above, then the quantity that we are after reduces to
<math display="block">\max P_X(x) \langle x | \mathcal{E}(\rho_B^x)|x \rangle~.</math>
We can interpret <math>\mathcal{E}</math> as a guessing strategy and this then reduces to the interpretation given above where an adversary wants to find the string <math>x</math> given access to quantum information via system <math>B</math>.
